newsitem.title: IRAQ: Jordan to take more Iraqi oil in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to take more Iraqi oil in 1997.

text.p: Jordan will buy 4.5 million tonnes of crude oil and refined oil products from Iraq in 1997, a senior Jordanian official said on Monday.
"...All together between crude oil and by-products, (we are buying) 4.5 million tonnes (for 1997)," Jordanian Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Hashem Dabbas told Reuters.
Dabbas, heading a high-ranking Jordanian trade team to Baghdad including Finance and Customs Minister Marwan Awad, arrived here late on Sunday.
The Jordanian delegation is the most senior official mission to Iraq since King Hussein last year turned against President Saddam Hussein after years of close ties.

No Jordanian official has been sent to Baghdad since September 1995 when former energy minister Samih Darwazah stroke an oil deal with Iraqi officials one month after senior Iraqis defected and were sheltered by King Hussein.
"(Our) relations will continue from better to best," Dabbas said.

Last year Jordan agreed with Iraq to buy oil estimated at 4.4 million tonnes -- an amount exempt from the United Nations trade sanctions that bar Iraq from exporting its oil following its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The Jordanian minister said this year's oil imports from Iraq would be more than last year's with "seven percent increase rate."

Jordan has been totally dependent on Iraq for its oil supplies since Saudi Arabia stopped the flow of an estimated 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude to punish it for its pro-Iraqi sympathy during the 1991 Gulf War.
Iraqi crude to Jordan is trucked by a fleet of about 2,000 tankers and Jordan imports 75,000 bpd from Iraq.
Amman pays market prices for 25,000 bpd and for another 25,000 bpd of products. The rest is at undisclosed concessionary terms.
Dabbas said: "We will also decide on the grant (of oil) which Iraq gives (to Jordan) free of charge."

The crude exports bring cash-strapped Iraq about $500 million a year. The amount is deposited in an escrow account at Jordan's Central Bank which pays almost half of it to finance Jordanian exports to Iraq.
Dabbas said they would discuss the trade volume between the two countries and would "reach a conclusion that will be acceptable for both sides."
The relations between the two countries have improved since Baghdad started limited oil sales nearly three weeks ago under an oil-for-food deal signed with the United Nations.
Under the deal Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion of oil every six months to buy food and medicine for Iraqis. Jordan wants to supply Baghdad with as much food and medicine as it can under the deal.

Earlier this month Iraqi Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh after meeting in Amman with the Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul- Karim al-Kabariti, told Jordanian industrialists that Iraq would give them "preference" to other international bidders who hope to supply Baghdad with urgent needs.
Dabbas said the delegation would meet with Iraq's Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed and Trade and Finance Minister Hikmat Mezban Ibrahim.
